title: Judges 1:9–15
context: After the action at Jerusalem, Judah goes down to fight the Canaanites in the hill country, in the South, and in the lowland. At Hebron, formerly Kiriath Arba, they strike Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. From there the campaign turns to Debir, formerly Kiriath Sepher. Caleb promises to give his daughter Achsah as wife to the man who strikes Kiriath Sepher and takes it. Othniel, the son of Kenaz, takes the city and receives her. When she comes, she urges a request for a field, alights from her donkey, and asks her father for a blessing and for springs of water in the South; Caleb gives her the upper springs and the lower springs. The unit closely parallels the Caleb–Othniel–Achsah report also found in Joshua 15. That correspondence is widely observed; how the episode sits next to the book’s opening “After the death of Joshua,” is discussed (a recap of earlier events, or a later telling of the same grant), and no single reconstruction should be treated as consensus. Both traditions read the passage as Caleb’s house receiving its inheritance under the earlier word, and as a family grant of water in a dry land. Othniel will appear again as a judge later in the book.

verses.text: After that, the children of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, and in the South, and in the lowland.
verses.arminianNotes:
After that, Judah went down to fight the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, and in the South, and in the lowland. The campaign now spreads across three regions of the lot.

Arminian readers hear a continued obedience to the command to go up. The fight is carried into hill, South, and lowland, not left at the one city just named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the three zones as the next stage of the work the LORD had delivered into Judah’s hand. The narrator maps the fight across the inheritance, not as a vague afterthought.

Both traditions read the verse as a geographic widening of Judah’s campaign, without inventing a dispute over the map.

verses.text: Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron. (The name of Hebron before that was Kiriath Arba.) They struck Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron. The name of Hebron before that was Kiriath Arba. They struck Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.

Arminian readers hear the old names and the three men as a concrete victory in a city long tied to promise and to fear. The same three will be called sons of Anak in verse 20.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the former name and the three who are struck. The verse records the fall of Hebron’s noted defenders, which verse 20 will place under Caleb in keeping with Moses’ word.

Both traditions take the notice as a real stroke against those names, shared ground with the later verse, not a contrast between the two readings.

verses.text: From there he went against the inhabitants of Debir. (The name of Debir before that was Kiriath Sepher.)
verses.arminianNotes:
From there he went against the inhabitants of Debir. The name of Debir before that was Kiriath Sepher. The campaign moves from Hebron to a second named city.

Arminian readers hear the advance continuing. Another town, under its older name, must actually be taken; the next verses will show how that taking is offered and done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the former-name notice as the narrator’s way of identifying Debir. The subject “he” looks toward the action Caleb will frame in verse 12.

Both traditions read the verse as the turn to Debir, shared narrative ground for the offer that follows.

verses.text: Caleb said, “I will give Achsah my daughter as wife to the man who strikes Kiriath Sepher, and takes it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Caleb said, “I will give Achsah my daughter as wife to the man who strikes Kiriath Sepher, and takes it.” The taking of the city is joined to a marriage promise in Caleb’s house.

Arminian readers hear a public charge that someone must actually strike and take the city. The offer is costly for Caleb’s family, and it is meant to get the work done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Caleb, already prominent in the earlier books, now frames the capture of Debir by a vowed gift of his daughter. The city is to be taken, and the marriage will seal that taking.

Both traditions take the vow as the means by which this town falls, not as a point of party contrast over marriage custom.

verses.text: Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took it, so he gave him Achsah his daughter as his wife.
verses.arminianNotes:
Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took it, so he gave him Achsah his daughter as his wife. The WEB presents Othniel as Kenaz’s son and, in this wording, as Caleb’s younger brother; some readers parse the family link a little differently, and that grammatical question is not settled here as a consensus.

Arminian readers hear a man who actually takes the city and so receives what was promised. The same Othniel will later be raised as a judge; his first appearance is already an act of courageous obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the capture and the marriage as the fulfillment of Caleb’s word. Whether one emphasizes Othniel’s sonship to Kenaz or his closeness to Caleb, the narrator’s point is that this man took Debir and was given Achsah.

Both traditions receive him as the taker of the city and as the man who will appear again in the book’s first judgeship, without forcing a fork over the exact kinship phrase.

verses.text: When she came, she got him to ask her father for a field. She got off her donkey; and Caleb said to her, “What would you like?”
verses.arminianNotes:
When she came, she got him to ask her father for a field. She got off her donkey; and Caleb said to her, “What would you like?” Achsah moves the request, and her father invites her to speak.

Arminian readers hear her initiative and Caleb’s open question. She is not a silent prize; she seeks a further gift, and he asks what she would like.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same movement: she urges the asking, alights, and is addressed by her father. The field she has in view will become, in the next verse, a request for water.

Both traditions take the verse as the approach that leads to the blessing, shared household narrative rather than a debate between the two readings.

verses.text: She said to him, “Give me a blessing; because you have set me in the land of the South, give me also springs of water.” Then Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verses.arminianNotes:
She said to him, “Give me a blessing; because you have set me in the land of the South, give me also springs of water.” Then Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.

Arminian readers hear a frank, practical plea. The South is dry, and she asks for water as a blessing; her father actually gives both the upper and the lower springs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same gift. Caleb does not refuse; he grants the springs that make the southern land livable, completing the inheritance in a father’s generosity.

Both traditions read the upper and lower springs as a real answer to a real need, shared ground in the family grant, without turning the water itself into a forced symbol.
